newsitem.title: FRANCE: France's Malraux reburied in Pantheon of heroes.
newsitem.headline: France's Malraux reburied in Pantheon of heroes.

text.p: French President Jacques Chirac led parties of the right and left in a tribute to cultural icon Andre Malraux on Saturday, reburying him in the Pantheon of national heroes in a ceremony laden with symbol and pomp.
As the neo-classical facade basked in white floodlights, six Republican Guards bore a coffin carrying the ashes of the writer, adventurer, orator and revolutionary into the imposing church.

For Chirac, the homage -- climax to a deluge of newspaper and magazine supplements on the writer -- was a chance to drape himself in the cloak of his mentor General Charles de Gaulle, whom Malraux served as culture minister.

"In truth, Andre Malraux, you more than any other embody Gaullism as the general wanted it -- neither of right nor left but of France," Chirac said in his eulogy 20 years to the day after Malraux's death.
"We are no longer in the 1960s but France, today like yesterday, can make its voice heard, defend its opinions, affirm its values -- above all peace and justice," Chirac said.
Malraux had been buried in Verrieres-le-Buisson, near Paris, where he had spent the last years of his life.

In a jibe at the far-right National Front, Culture Minister Philippe Douste-Blazy said Malraux "embodied French genius without yielding to nationalism". Douste-Blazy had on Friday boycotted a book fair in Toulon over criticism of Jewish writer Marek Halter by the city's Front mayor.
Foreign guests attending the Latin Quarter ceremony includes Peru's Mario Vargas Llosa, Briton V.S. Naipaul, Israel's Amos Oz and Spain's Jorge Semprun.

In a show designed by a painter, more than 100 students dressed in raincoats from the Andre-Malraux school bore blown-up photographs retracing the French writer's life along the torch-lit Rue Soufflot. Loudspeakers relayed extracts from his fiery, theatrical speeches.

As culture minister throughout De Gaulle's presidency from 1959 to 1969, Malraux is remembered for launching an acclaimed clean-up of Paris landmarks, including Notre Dame cathedral, and dotting France with Maisons de la Culture (cultural centres).
Four green statues of cats from Ancient Egypt had been placed around the coffin, a reminder of Malraux' fondness for the animals and of his passion for Egyptian art.
Malraux travelled extensively in the Far East, fought on the Republican side in the Spanish Civil War and narrowly escaped a German firing squad as a World War Two Resistance fighter.

He drew on his own adventures for his best-known works: "La Condition Humaine" (Man's Estate) about revolutionary tension in China in the 1920s, and "L'Espoir" (Days of Hope) after setting up a squadron of foreign volunteer pilots for the Republicans in Spain's 1936-39 Civil War.

The last national heroes to be reburied in the Pantheon were Nobel prize-winning physicist Marie Curie -- the first woman to earn such an honour on her own merits -- and her scientist husband Pierre. The late president Francois Mitterrand presided over that ceremony shortly before leaving office.

Malraux was laid to rest next to Jean Moulin, the wartime Resistance hero tortured to death by the Nazis whom he eulogised in a vibrant speech in 1964 when Moulin's remains were reburied in the Pantheon.
